**InstructGPT (2203.02155)** aligns GPT-3 through a pipeline of supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, training a reward model on labeler comparisons, and optimizing a policy against that reward model with PPO [c1115][c1130]. The data comes from about 40 contractors selected through a screening test, plus prompts submitted to the OpenAI API [c1115][c1135]. Labelers significantly preferred InstructGPT outputs to GPT-3 outputs, with 175B InstructGPT preferred 85 ± 3% of the time [c1153].

**Constitutional AI (2212.08073)** replaces human harmlessness labels with AI feedback. The supervised stage generates responses to harmful prompts, has the model critique them against constitutional principles, revises them, and fine-tunes on the revisions [c3422]. The RL stage uses AI-generated preference labels, produced by asking which response is best under a constitutional principle, to train a preference model for RL from AI feedback [c3423]. Human feedback is still used for helpfulness labels [c3412][c3460].

**Anthropic's helpful-and-harmless RLHF (2204.05862)** collects separate crowdworker datasets for helpfulness and for red-teaming harmfulness, where workers choose the more helpful or more harmful response at each turn [c3525][c3549]. Preference models trained on these comparisons serve as reward signals for RLHF [c3569]. Mixed helpful-and-harmless training lets preference models behave helpfully while encouraging polite refusal of harmful requests [c3527]. Iterated online training, which re-deploys updated models roughly weekly, significantly improved crowdworker preference [c3529][c3587].

**LIMA (2305.11206)** uses no RL or preference modeling. It fine-tunes LLaMa 65B with the standard supervised loss on 1,000 curated prompt-response examples, drawn from community forums and manually written examples [c3729][c3739]. In a human study, LIMA responses were either equivalent or strictly preferred to GPT-4 in 43% of cases [c3727]. The authors read this as support for the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis, that pretraining supplies most of the knowledge [c3741].

**FLAN (2109.01652)** instruction-tunes a 137B pretrained model on over 60 NLP datasets verbalized via natural-language instruction templates [c2928][c2935]. Each dataset receives ten unique instruction templates [c2936]. Evaluation is zero-shot on held-out task clusters, where FLAN beats zero-shot GPT-3 on 20 of 25 datasets [c2928][c2932].

**Comparison.** InstructGPT and Anthropic's HH RLHF both train reward or preference models on human comparison labels, and both then optimize a policy with RL [c1130][c3569]. Constitutional AI keeps this RL structure but generates harmlessness comparison labels from the model under written principles [c3423]. LIMA uses a small set of curated supervised examples with no reward model, and FLAN uses large, template-verbalized public datasets with no reward model [c3729][c2935]. The library contains no shared-benchmark head-to-head comparison among these methods, so claims about relative effectiveness are limited to what each paper reports.

**Research Brief: Token order, sequence length, and long-context use across Transformer, RoPE, and Mamba**

**1. Original Transformer: token order and sequence length**
The Transformer contains no recurrence or convolution, so it must inject order information explicitly. It adds "positional encodings" to the input embeddings, using sine and cosine functions of different frequencies [c15]. The authors chose this form because it may let the model learn to attend by relative positions and may extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen in training [c15]. Learned positional embeddings gave nearly identical results to the base model [c15][c28]. Self-attention connects all positions with a constant number of sequential operations, though averaging attention-weighted positions reduces effective resolution [c5][c16]. Decoder self-attention is masked to preserve the auto-regressive property [c12].

**2. RoPE (RoFormer): token order and sequence length**
RoPE encodes absolute position with a rotation matrix and incorporates explicit relative-position dependency into the self-attention formulation [c2142][c2145]. Its stated properties include sequence-length flexibility and attention between tokens that decays as relative distance grows [c2142][c2145]. Unlike additive position embeddings, RoPE is multiplicative: relative position arises from the product of rotated query and key vectors [c2155]. On long-text classification, RoFormer's accuracy rose with longer maximum input lengths in pre-training [c2183], and at input length 1024 it outperformed WoBERT by an absolute 1.5% on CAIL2019-SCM, while being comparable at 512 [c2185]. The brief's evidence does not establish RoPE's behaviour beyond the lengths tested.

**3. Mamba: token order and sequence length**
Mamba is a selective state space model with no attention or MLP blocks [c4191]. Its SSM parameters are functions of the input, letting it selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence [c4191]. It scales linearly in sequence length [c4191][c4258]. On a synthetic induction-heads-style task, it generalised perfectly to million-length sequences, about 4000× longer than training, while no other method exceeded 2× [c4232]. In scaling experiments, Mamba matched a strong Transformer++ recipe, particularly as sequence length grew [c4234]. The reported 5× inference throughput over Transformers [c4191] is consistent with the linear-time design.

**4. "Lost in the Middle": how models use long contexts**
Across multi-document QA and key-value retrieval, performance is highest when relevant information sits at the start or end of the input and degrades when it is in the middle, a U-shaped curve [c2781][c2775][c2790]. This holds even for explicitly long-context models [c2775]. It also holds for GPT-4, whose absolute performance is higher, and for Llama-2 variants [c2821][c2822]. The authors conclude that current models do not robustly access and use information across long inputs [c2781][c2778].

**Comparison and conclusion**
The three architectures handle order differently: the original Transformer adds sinusoidal encodings, RoPE rotates queries and keys, and Mamba makes state transitions input-dependent. Evidence for length generalisation is strongest for Mamba on a synthetic task and for RoFormer on classification up to 1024 tokens. "Lost in the Middle" shows that even with long windows, retrieval within a context remains position-sensitive. The brief's evidence does not directly test whether RoPE or Mamba avoid this U-shaped effect; that gap is not covered by the library.

text:
**Research Brief**

**1. Original Transformer: token order and sequence length**

The Transformer contains no recurrence and no convolution, so it must inject positional information explicitly: "positional encodings" are added to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks [c15]. The authors used sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, which they hypothesized would let the model attend by relative positions, and which may allow extrapolation to sequence lengths longer than those seen in training [c15]. Learned positional embeddings gave nearly identical results [c15]. Regarding length, self-attention connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, and is computationally faster than recurrence when sequence length is smaller than representation dimensionality [c16][c17]. The paper also notes that restricting self-attention to a neighborhood would reduce cost for very long sequences, which was left as future work [c17].

**2. RoPE (RoFormer): token order and sequence length**

RoPE encodes absolute position with a rotation matrix while incorporating explicit relative-position dependency in the self-attention formulation [c2142][c2152]. The rotary matrix uses pre-defined parameters θi = 10000^(−2(i−1)/d), and the approach is multiplicative rather than additive [c2155]. The paper reports properties including flexibility in sequence length, decaying inter-token dependency as relative distance increases, and compatibility with linear self-attention [c2142]. On pre-training, RoFormer's accuracy rose with an increasing upper bound on sequence length, which the authors attribute to the generalizability of RoPE [c2183]. The library's evidence does not establish how RoPE compares to the original Transformer on very long inputs beyond these reported results.

**3. Mamba: token order and sequence length**

Mamba is built on selective state space models whose SSM parameters are functions of the input, which lets it selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence depending on the current token [c4191]. It uses a hardware-aware parallel algorithm, and its computation and memory scale linearly in sequence length during training, with constant time per step during autoregressive inference [c4196]. The paper reports performance improving on real data up to million-length sequences [c4191][c4196], and about 5× higher inference throughput than Transformers [c4191]. The library's evidence does not describe an explicit positional encoding mechanism for Mamba.

**4. "Lost in the Middle": how models use long contexts**

The study finds that changing the position of relevant information in the input context substantially affects performance, indicating that current language models do not robustly access and use information in long inputs [c2781]. Performance shows a U-shaped curve: highest when relevant information is at the very beginning (primacy bias) or end (recency bias), and significantly degraded when it sits in the middle [c2781][c2790]. This holds even for explicitly long-context models [c2775]. The pattern persists in GPT-4, which achieves higher absolute performance but still degrades for middle-positioned information [c2821].

**Comparison and conclusion**

The original Transformer and RoPE both add position information explicitly (sinusoidal encodings versus rotary relative encoding) [c15][c2142], while Mamba's selection mechanism makes its recurrence input-dependent [c4191]. The library reports length-generalization claims for each, but does not directly test them against one another. "Lost in the Middle" shows that even long-context models fail to use middle-of-context information reliably [c2775][c2781], so long nominal context length does not by itself guarantee robust use of that context. The library does not contain a direct experimental comparison of these three architectures on this positional-robustness question.

**Research Brief: Evaluation of LLM Systems and Agents**

**MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena (2306.05685).** MT-bench is a set of open-ended questions evaluating a chatbot's multi-turn conversational and instruction-following ability, constructed to differentiate chatbots on core capabilities such as reasoning and math [c2861]. Chatbot Arena is a crowdsourced platform with anonymous battles, where users converse with two chatbots and rate responses by personal preference [c2861]. Both rely on human ratings as the primary metric, and the paper proposes "LLM-as-a-judge" as a scalable substitute, since human evaluation is slow and costly [c2861][c2868]. Reported findings: strong LLM judges reach over 80% agreement, on par with human-expert agreement [c2893]. The authors recommend evaluating models with both human-preference benchmarks and standardized benchmarks, since no single benchmark determines model quality [c2889][c2890]. Stated limitations concern the scope of the study: MT-bench is small-scale with controlled human evaluation, while Chatbot Arena is larger-scale with crowdsourced, in-the-wild judgments [c2880]. The library passages do not detail specific biases of the LLM judges beyond these agreement figures.

**MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (LLM-as-a-judge).** Reference-based metrics like ROUGE/BLEU are ineffective for open-ended chat questions [c2868]. MT-Bench is a multi-turn question set; Chatbot Arena is a crowdsourced battle platform [c2856]. GPT-4 as judge reaches over 80% agreement with humans, on par with human-human agreement [c2893][c2856]. The paper reports position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases, plus limited reasoning ability, and says some biases are minor or can be mitigated [c2862][c2856]. The authors recommend a hybrid framework combining capability benchmarks with preference-based LLM judging [c2862].

**Ragas (RAG evaluation).** Ragas is a reference-free framework for RAG pipelines and requires no ground-truth human annotations [c2830]. It scores faithfulness (is the answer grounded in the retrieved context), answer relevance, and context relevance [c2846]. It was compared with a GPT Score baseline, where ChatGPT assigns 0–10 scores per dimension [c2846]. The library does not contain passages describing Ragas' own weaknesses or biases, so I cannot report them.

**SWE-bench (coding agents).** It contains 2,294 issues drawn from real GitHub issues and pull requests across 12 Python repositories; the model must edit the codebase to resolve the issue [c2643]. Tasks require coordinating changes across functions and files and handling long contexts [c2652]. Evaluation is execution-based, but the authors note that passing tests is insufficient, since LM-generated code can be less comprehensive, efficient, or readable than human solutions [c2675]. Performance is low: the best model, Claude 2, solved 1.96% of issues [c2643]. The collection process can be applied to new repositories, allowing evaluation on issues created after a model's training date [c2652].

**AgentBench (LLMs as agents).** It has 8 interactive environments across 3 types and evaluates 29 API-based and open-source LLMs [c4473]. Top commercial models clearly outperform many open-source models no larger than 70B [c4473]. The predominant failure is "Task Limit Exceeded," indicating weak reasoning and decision-making; other failures include invalid formats and invalid actions [c4505]. Code training has mixed effects, helping some agent tasks while harming others [c4473].

**Conclusion.** The benchmarks measure different layers: MT-Bench/Arena measure conversational preference, Ragas measures RAG component quality, SWE-bench measures repository-level issue resolution, and AgentBench measures multi-environment agent behaviour. Their main caveats are judge bias (MT-Bench), test-passing not equalling code quality (SWE-bench), and long-horizon reasoning failures (AgentBench). The library does not cover Ragas' limitations.

# Research Brief: Position Handling in Transformer, RoPE, and Mamba, and Long-Context Use

## 1. Original Transformer: token order and sequence length

The Transformer has no recurrence and no convolution. To make use of sequence order, the authors add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks [c15]. They use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, with wavelengths forming a geometric progression from 2π to 10000·2π [c15]. The stated rationale is that for any fixed offset k, PE(pos+k) can be represented as a linear function of PE(pos), which should make attention by relative position easy to learn [c15]. The authors chose the sinusoidal form because it may allow extrapolation to sequences longer than those seen in training, and they report that learned positional embeddings produced nearly identical results [c15].

Self-attention connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) [c16]. In terms of computation, self-attention is faster than recurrent layers when sequence length n is smaller than representation dimensionality d [c16][c17]. For very long sequences, the authors suggest restricting self-attention to a neighbourhood of size r, which would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r) [c17].

## 2. RoPE (RoFormer): encoding relative position in attention

RoPE encodes absolute position with a rotation matrix and incorporates explicit relative-position dependency into the self-attention formulation [c2142][c2145]. The authors describe the approach as multiplicative rather than additive, with relative position arising through the rotation-matrix product [c2155]. The paper lists properties including sequence-length flexibility, decay of inter-token dependency as relative distance grows, and compatibility with linear self-attention [c2145][c2142]. In pre-training, RoFormer replaces the sinusoidal encoding of the baseline with RoPE and uses a maximum sequence length of 512 [c2171]. The authors report that accuracy rises with an increasing upper bound on sequence length, which they attribute to the generalisability of RoPE [c2183]. They also report faster convergence in pre-training and better performance on long-text tasks [c2187].

## 3. Mamba: linear-time sequence modelling

Mamba is attention-free. Its SSM parameters are functions of the input, so the model can selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence depending on the current token [c4191]. The authors present this as addressing the inability of earlier subquadratic models to perform content-based reasoning [c4191]. Mamba is described as having linear scaling in sequence length [c4191]. It achieves about 5× higher generation throughput than Transformers of similar size [c4197][c4249]. On a selective-copying task it generalises to million-length sequences, roughly 4000× longer than seen in training [c4232]. Its pretraining perplexity improves as context grows up to 1M, whereas the HyenaDNA model gets worse with sequence length [c4242].

## 4. "Lost in the Middle": how models use long contexts

The paper studies how language models use information in long input contexts. It finds that performance can degrade significantly when the position of relevant information changes [c2781]. It reports a U-shaped curve: performance is highest when relevant information is at the very beginning (primacy bias) or end (recency bias) of the context, and degrades significantly when models must use information in the middle [c2781][c2790]. This holds even for explicitly long-context models [c2778][c2781]. GPT-4 achieves the highest absolute performance among the models evaluated but still shows the U-shaped curve [c2821]. The authors conclude that current language models do not robustly make use of information in long input contexts [c2775].

## Comparison and conclusion

The three approaches differ in how they handle order. The original Transformer adds fixed sinusoidal encodings to the input [c15]. RoPE builds relative position into attention through a rotation matrix [c2145]. Mamba dispenses with attention and uses input-dependent recurrence with linear scaling in sequence length [c4191]. The length evidence is reported separately for each: the Transformer's self-attention connects positions in a constant number of sequential operations [c16], RoFormer reports accuracy gains as the sequence-length bound increases [c2183], and Mamba reports performance gains with context up to million-length sequences [c4242]. The "Lost in the Middle" study shows that, for language models in general, using information from the middle of a long input is a documented weakness [c2775][c2781]. The library does not contain any evidence testing the original Transformer, RoFormer, or Mamba on the "Lost in the Middle" protocol, so the sources provided do not establish how these three specific architectures perform on that test.

text:
**MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena (LLM-as-a-judge, paper 2306.05685)**
MT-Bench is a set of open-ended multi-turn questions testing conversational and instruction-following ability and core capabilities such as reasoning and math; Chatbot Arena is a crowdsourced platform of anonymous battles where users rate responses [c2861]. Because human rating is slow and costly, the paper uses strong LLMs (e.g., GPT-4) as judges and reports over 80% agreement with human preferences, comparable to human-human agreement [c2856][c2862]. The judge is compared against human expert and crowd votes, with agreement measured in pairwise and single-answer grading setups [c2880][c2885]. Reported weaknesses: position bias, verbosity bias (a "repetitive list" attack succeeded against all judges, though GPT-4 defended better), self-enhancement bias, and limited reasoning ability [c2862][c2873][c2874]. Position bias was tested via swapped-order consistency and a math-correctness test where judges failed on some items [c2871].

**Ragas (paper 2309.15217)**
Ragas is a reference-free framework for RAG pipelines measuring faithfulness (claims supported by context, scored as supported statements over total statements), answer relevance (generated questions compared with the original via embedding similarity), and context relevance (fraction of context sentences needed to answer) [c2838][c2839][c2840][c2844]. Agreement with human annotators on WikiEval pairwise comparisons is high for faithfulness and answer relevance, but lower for answer relevance due to subtle differences, and context relevance is the hardest dimension, with ChatGPT often failing to select crucial sentences from long contexts [c2845]. The metrics rely on an LLM judge (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k), so they inherit LLM judging limitations [c2839].

**SWE-bench (paper 2310.06770)**
SWE-bench evaluates whether a model can generate a pull request that resolves a real GitHub issue and passes its fail-to-pass tests, built from 12 Python repositories through attribute filtering and execution-based validation [c2647][c2648][c2649]. Results are reported as resolve rates: Claude 2 resolves only 1.96% of issues with BM25 retrieval [c2646][c2662]. Reported weaknesses include difficulty that correlates with context length, models struggling to localize problematic code, and poorly formatted patches; models tend to produce shorter edits than gold patches [c2663][c2666][c2722].

**AgentBench (paper 2308.03688)**
AgentBench evaluates LLMs-as-agents across 8 interactive environments grouped as Code, Game, and Web, with success rate as the main metric (step success rate and task success rate for web tasks) [c4481][c4615]. It reports a substantial gap between top commercial models and open-source models up to 70B [c4473]. Reported failure analysis attributes problems to poor long-term reasoning, decision-making, and instruction following [c4473]; open-source models show more invalid-format (10.4% vs 6.0%) and invalid-action (13.6% vs 4.6%) outcomes than commercial ones [c4623]. Task Limit Exceeded trajectories are dominated by repetition of earlier content [c4638]. The paper also notes code training has mixed effects across agent tasks [c4473].

**Comparison.** MT-Bench/Arena and Ragas both use LLM judges, with reported position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases for the former and reliance on a judge LLM for the latter. SWE-bench and AgentBench use execution-based or environment-based success metrics, with weaknesses centred on context handling, instruction following, and repetition rather than judge bias. Note that the library does not include evidence on self-enhancement bias quantitatively for Ragas or on how AgentBench's environments were validated beyond what is cited above.

**MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena (LLM-as-a-judge).** The paper proposes using strong LLMs as judges of open-ended chat-assistant answers, validated against human preferences from 58 experts on MT-bench and thousands of crowd users on Chatbot Arena [c2893][c2880]. Strong LLM judges such as GPT-4 are reported to match both controlled and crowdsourced human preferences, achieving over 80% agreement, the same level as human-human agreement [c2856][c2862]. Reported biases and limitations: position bias, where a judge favors one answer position [c2871]; verbosity bias, demonstrated with a "repetitive list" attack that all tested judges are prone to, though GPT-4 defends significantly better [c2874]; self-enhancement bias, where GPT-4 favors itself by about 10% and Claude-v1 by about 25% in win rate, but the authors say their data cannot determine whether models exhibit this bias [c2875]; and limited reasoning ability [c2856].

**Ragas (RAG evaluation).** Ragas is a reference-free framework for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation on faithfulness, answer relevance and context relevance, with each computed by prompting an LLM [c2830][c2838][c2839][c2844]. On the WikiEval dataset, its predictions agree with human judgments more closely than the GPT Score and GPT Ranking baselines, with faithfulness and answer relevance aligning most closely [c2845]. Context relevance was the hardest dimension, as ChatGPT often struggled to select the crucial sentences from the context, especially for longer contexts [c2845].

**SWE-bench (software engineering).** It contains 2,294 task instances from real GitHub issues and pull requests across 12 Python repositories; models must generate a patch that passes the associated tests [c2643][c2647]. Performance is very low: the best model, Claude 2, resolves 1.96% of issues with BM25 retrieval, and 4.8% with oracle retrieval [c2662]. The authors note that execution-based testing alone cannot guarantee generated code is comprehensive, efficient or readable [c2675].

**AgentBench (LLM as agent).** It spans 8 interactive environments across code, game and web groundings, evaluating 29 API-based and open-source LLMs [c4473][c4481]. Results show a significant performance gap between top commercial models and many open-source models no larger than 70B [c4473]. The predominant failure cause is Task Limit Exceeded, indicating weak reasoning and decision-making, while Invalid Format and Invalid Action errors reflect poor instruction following [c4505][c4487]. The authors report that code training has ambivalent effects, improving some agent tasks while harming others [c4485].

**Comparison.** The library does not contain a direct comparison of these four systems' evaluation methods, so no cross-benchmark conclusion is drawn here. Within each source, the reported weaknesses are: judge biases for MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena and Ragas [c2875][c2845]; very low absolute success rates and limits of execution-based testing for SWE-bench [c2662][c2675]; and task-limit failures and instruction-following errors for AgentBench [c4505].

## Research Brief: Architectures of LLM-Based Agents (MemGPT, Generative Agents, AutoGen, HuggingGPT)

**Memory**

- **MemGPT** is explicitly OS-inspired: it uses a memory hierarchy and control flow analogous to traditional operating systems to manage limited context windows, giving the illusion of larger context resources [c2318]. A FIFO queue and recall storage (the message database) hold incoming messages and generated outputs; messages are paged back into context via function calls [c2294]. In conversational evaluation, MemGPT retains full conversation history and retrieves it through paginated search, outperforming baselines that see only lossy summaries [c2304].
- **Generative Agents** and **AutoGen**: the provided passages do not describe their memory mechanisms. The library lists Generative Agents [2304.03442] but no retrieved passage covers its memory design, so this cannot be stated from the evidence.

**Planning**

- **HuggingGPT** uses a global planning strategy: it obtains the entire task queue within one query. Iterative planning (as in AutoGPT/BabyAGI) generates the next task step by step and can require many LLM queries and loop endlessly if one step errs; global planning always yields a solution in one query but cannot guarantee per-step correctness or plan optimality [c2615]. Task-planning difficulty grows with task range [c2615].
- **MemGPT** planning is not described in the passages beyond its event-based control flow, which is mentioned as enabling unbounded context handling [c2294].
- **AutoGen** supports both static (predefined agent order) and dynamic conversation patterns [c2459].

**Coordination**

- **AutoGen** is a generic multi-agent infrastructure. Its `ConversableAgent` is the base abstraction; `AssistantAgent` (LLM-backed) and `UserProxyAgent` (human/tool-backed) are pre-configured subclasses, and they cooperate by passing solutions and feedback, with the user proxy executing code [c2431]. Conversation patterns can be static or dynamic, with optional human involvement [c2459].
- **HuggingGPT** coordinates by using the LLM as a controller that dispatches tasks to expert models from Hugging Face, focused on AI-area tasks [c2614][c2616].
- **Generative Agents** and **MemGPT** multi-agent coordination: not covered by the provided passages.

**Comparison and Conclusion**

HuggingGPT is the most explicit about planning (global, one-shot task queue), AutoGen about coordination (generic, configurable multi-agent conversation), and MemGPT about memory (OS-style paging over a finite context) [c2615][c2431][c2318]. Each design trades off between task depth and range [c2616]. The evidence supplied is insufficient to compare Generative Agents on any of the three dimensions, and the evidence does not cover the memory and multi-agent coordination of MemGPT and Generative Agents respectively; retrieving those papers' passages would be needed to complete the comparison.

**Brief: Architectures of four LLM-based agent systems**

**MemGPT (memory-centric).** Memory is the core design. MemGPT uses an OS-inspired hierarchy: "main context" (in-prompt, analogous to RAM) and "external context" (out-of-window storage, analogous to disk) [c2295]. The LLM manages its own memory via function calls that move data between tiers, and can chain calls by requesting follow-up inference ("request heartbeat=true") to perform multi-step retrieval [c2295]. A queue manager writes incoming messages and outputs to recall storage and manages the FIFO queue [c2294]. Planning is not a separate module; the paper emphasizes self-directed memory editing and retrieval, guided by instructions describing the hierarchy and a function schema [c2296]. Coordination is not a focus of the paper; its evaluation covers document analysis and conversational agents [c2318].

**Generative Agents (memory, reflection, planning per agent).** The architecture has three components: a memory stream (a natural-language log of experiences), reflection (synthesizing memories into higher-level inferences), and planning (turning conclusions and the environment into high-level plans, then recursively into detailed actions) [c2326]. Retrieval combines relevance, recency, and importance [c2326]. Plans and reflections are written back into the memory stream [c2326]. Agents run an action loop: at each step they perceive, store observations, and prompt the LLM to decide whether to continue or react to the current plan [c2367]. Multi-agent coordination happens through a shared simulated society, and the ablation study shows each memory type contributes to believability [c2380].

**AutoGen (conversation-based coordination).** AutoGen's core units are customizable "conversable" agents that can use LLMs, humans, tools, or combinations [c2426]. Coordination is via "conversation programming": computation (agent actions) and control flow (which agent speaks next) are both driven by inter-agent conversation [c2435]. Dynamic flows are supported through custom reply functions, LLM-driven function calls, and a GroupChatManager that selects the next speaker [c2437]. The paper describes no separate long-term memory module; memory is effectively the conversation history. Planning emerges from agent dialogue rather than an explicit planner.

**HuggingGPT (LLM as central planner/controller).** A single LLM controller runs four stages: task planning (parsing the request into a task list with dependencies), model selection, task execution by expert models, and response generation [c2576]. Model selection is an in-context choice over expert-model descriptions, filtered by task type and ranked by downloads, with top-K candidates kept to fit the context [c2587]. Coordination is hierarchical and centralized: the LLM routes subtasks to experts and integrates their results [c2579]. The paper does not describe a persistent memory mechanism beyond the workflow logs used for the final response [c2576].

**Comparison.** The four systems differ mainly in where they put the emphasis. MemGPT addresses memory most directly, with a tiered store the LLM controls itself. Generative Agents has the richest model of memory-driven planning, through retrieval, reflection, and recursive plans. AutoGen centers coordination, with dialogue as the control mechanism and little built-in memory. HuggingGPT is a centralized planner-executor for multimodal tool use, with no long-term memory described. The library does not contain a direct quantitative comparison among these four systems, so this comparison rests on each paper's own description of its design.

**Research Brief: Evaluation of LLM Systems and Agents**

**MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (LLM-as-a-judge).** These benchmarks evaluate chat assistants on open-ended questions, where rule-based or reference-based metrics are ineffective [c2868]. MT-Bench is a series of open-ended questions assessing multi-turn conversational and instruction-following ability, and Chatbot Arena is a crowdsourced platform of anonymous battles between chatbots [c2862]. Strong LLM judges such as GPT-4 reach over 80% agreement with human preferences, comparable to human-human agreement [c2856][c2862]. Reported biases include position bias (favoring certain response positions), verbosity bias (favoring longer answers), and self-enhancement bias [c2871][c2873][c2874][c2875]. The authors find self-enhancement effects are not conclusively established given limited data [c2875]. Judges also show limited reasoning ability, and all tested LLM judges, though GPT-4 defends better than others, may be prone to verbosity bias under a "repetitive list" attack [c2874]. Mitigations exist for some biases [c2862].

**Ragas (reference-free RAG evaluation).** Ragas evaluates retrieval-augmented generation along three dimensions: faithfulness, answer relevance, and context relevance, without requiring ground-truth annotations [c2830][c2838]. Faithfulness is computed as the fraction of answer statements supported by the context [c2838]. On the WikiEval dataset, Ragas predictions are reported as closely aligned with human judgments, especially for faithfulness and answer relevance [c2847][c2846]. The library does not contain further information on Ragas weaknesses or biases.

**SWE-bench (software engineering).** SWE-bench draws task instances from real GitHub issues and merged pull requests across 12 Python repositories [c2643][c2650]. Models must generate a patch that passes repository tests tied to the issue [c2647][c2649]. Performance is low: the best model, Claude 2, resolves only 1.96% of issues [c2643]. The authors note that execution-based testing alone cannot guarantee quality, since model-generated code can be less comprehensive, efficient, or readable than human solutions [c2675]. The benchmark is limited to Python [c2675].

**AgentBench (LLM-as-agent).** AgentBench spans eight environments across code, game, and web groundings, evaluated over 29 LLMs [c4481][c4473]. Success rate is the main metric for environments such as house-holding [c4494]. Across models, the predominant failure is Task Limit Exceeded, indicating weak long-horizon reasoning and decision-making [c4505]. Invalid Format and Invalid Action errors are reported as more frequent for open-source models (10.4% and 13.6%) than commercial ones (6.0% and 4.6%) [c4623]. The authors also report that code training has mixed effects on agent tasks [c4473].

**Comparison.** The frameworks target different aspects: MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena assess human-preference alignment in chat, Ragas assesses RAG pipeline quality, SWE-bench assesses patch correctness on real repositories, and AgentBench assesses task success across interactive environments [c2856][c2830][c2643][c4481]. Each relies on a proxy for the ideal judgment: LLM judges stand in for human raters [c2856], and repository test suites serve as the executable check on patches [c2647]. The library does not contain further comparative analysis of these frameworks.

# Research Brief: Architectures for LLM-Based Agents

## MemGPT: Memory
MemGPT uses an OS-inspired hierarchy: "main context" (prompt tokens, analogous to RAM) and "external context" (analogous to disk) [c2295]. Main context is split into read-only system instructions, a read/write working context, and a FIFO queue [c2293]. External storage includes recall storage and archival storage [c2294][c2297]. The LLM manages its own memory through function calls that move data between tiers [c2295][c2292]. A queue manager issues a "memory pressure" warning at 70% of the window and flushes the queue at 100%, keeping a recursive summary of evicted messages [c2297][c2293].

## MemGPT: Planning and Coordination
MemGPT's control flow is event-based. The LLM can chain function calls by requesting immediate follow-up inference, which enables multi-step retrieval [c2295]. Function calls also manage control flow between context management, response generation and user interaction [c2290].

## Generative Agents: Memory
The memory stream is a long-term record of experiences in natural language [c2326]. Retrieval scores memories by recency, relevance and importance, normalised to [0,1] and combined with equal weights [c2359][c2360]. Relevance uses embedding cosine similarity [c2359]. Importance is scored by the LLM on a 1–10 scale [c2360]. Reflection synthesises memories into higher-level inferences when importance scores exceed a threshold, producing trees of reflections [c2363].

## Generative Agents: Planning and Coordination
Planning translates conclusions and the environment into high-level action plans, recursively refined into detailed behaviour, with outputs fed back into memory [c2326]. Coordination among agents is not detailed in the retrieved passages beyond the aim of a "small, interactive society of agents" [c2326].

## AutoGen: Memory
The retrieved passages do not describe AutoGen's memory mechanism.

## AutoGen: Planning and Coordination
AutoGen builds on conversable agents that can be LLM-, tool-, or human-backed, and on conversation programming [c2426]. Agents share a unified send/receive and generate-reply interface, with auto-reply mechanisms that drive conversation without a separate control plane [c2436]. Control can be natural-language (e.g. a "TERMINATE" instruction), programming-language, or a mix [c2436]. Dynamic group chat uses a GroupChatManager that selects the next speaker, collects a response and broadcasts it [c2447]. A pilot study found role-play speaker-selection prompts gave higher success rates and fewer LLM calls than task-style prompts [c2501][c2502].

## HuggingGPT: Memory
Chat logs are included in the planning prompt so that user-mentioned resources can be traced across multi-turn dialogue [c2586]. Beyond this, the retrieved passages do not describe a dedicated memory mechanism.

## HuggingGPT: Planning and Coordination
HuggingGPT uses an LLM as controller in four stages: task planning, model selection, task execution and response generation [c2576][c2580]. Planning parses the request into a task list with execution order and resource dependencies, using demonstrations [c2586]. Model selection filters candidates by task type, ranks by Hugging Face downloads, and keeps the top-K in context [c2587]. Expert models execute tasks, and parallel or serial execution follows dependencies [c2613].

## Comparison
MemGPT and Generative Agents address memory most directly, with MemGPT handling it through paging between tiers and Generative Agents through scored retrieval plus reflection. AutoGen and HuggingGPT centre on coordination: AutoGen through conversation among agents, HuggingGPT through a central LLM planner dispatching to experts. The library does not cover AutoGen's memory, or detailed coordination in Generative Agents.

**Research brief: distinguishing GPT-3, LLaMA, Llama 2, PaLM and Mistral 7B**

Note: The library contains no paper on GPT-3 or PaLM as primary sources. Their details here come only from how other papers describe them, so the coverage is partial.

**GPT-3.** The library has no primary paper for GPT-3. The evidence only describes it as a comparison point: LLaMA-13B "outperforms GPT-3 on most benchmarks despite being 10× smaller" [c750][c766], and Llama 2 70B is "close to GPT-3.5" on MMLU and GSM8K [c840]. Its main contribution, scale, and training emphasis cannot be stated from the provided passages.

**LLaMA.** The focus is training models that achieve the best possible performance at various inference budgets, by training on more tokens than is typical. Models range from 7B to 65B parameters [c750]. Its distinguishing feature is the use of only publicly available data, which makes the work compatible with open-sourcing, unlike Chinchilla, PaLM, or GPT-3 [c750]. LLaMA-65B is competitive with Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B [c793][c766].

**Llama 2.** A family of pretrained and fine-tuned models at 7B to 70B parameters, with competitiveness against existing open-source chat models and some proprietary ones, though it still lags behind GPT-4 [c937]. Its emphasis is on alignment with helpfulness and safety [c937]. The 70B model is close to GPT-3.5 on MMLU and GSM8K but has a significant gap on coding, and it is on par or better than PaLM (540B) on almost all benchmarks [c840]. The 70B chat model has a 36% win rate and 31.5% tie rate against ChatGPT in human evaluation [c875].

**PaLM.** The library has no primary PaLM paper. It appears only as a comparison: Llama 2 70B is on par or better than PaLM (540B) on almost all benchmarks [c840], and LLaMA-65B surpasses PaLM-540B on nearly all benchmarks except BoolQ and WinoGrande [c766]. Its training approach is not covered by the provided evidence.

**Mistral 7B.** A 7B-parameter model with an efficiency emphasis. It outperforms Llama 2 13B on all metrics and approaches Code-Llama 7B's code performance without sacrificing non-code performance [c2131]. On reasoning and STEM (MMLU), it mirrors what a Llama 2 model over 3× its size would achieve, but its knowledge-benchmark compression is lower (1.9×), likely due to its limited parameter count [c2131]. It is superior to Llama 1 34B in mathematics, code, and reasoning [c2130].

**Comparison.** LLaMA and Llama 2 are distinguished by open, publicly sourced data and a range of sizes, with Llama 2 adding a safety/alignment emphasis. Mistral 7B is distinguished by strong per-parameter efficiency at a small scale. GPT-3 and PaLM are represented in the library only as benchmarks against which the open models are measured, so their own contributions cannot be summarised from these passages.

**Research brief: five LLM families**

**GPT-3 (2005.14165).** The main contribution is showing that scale enables in-context learning. The authors train "a 175 billion parameter autoregressive language model" and evaluate it in few-shot, one-shot, and zero-shot settings, with as many demonstrations as fit the context window in the few-shot case [c572]. Training emphasis is on in-context adaptation rather than fine-tuning, which the authors leave to future work [c572]. On LAMBADA, GPT-3 175B advances the state of the art by 18% [c599].

**LLaMA (2302.13971).** LLaMA is a collection of foundation models from 7B to 65B parameters, trained on trillions of tokens [c749]. The emphasis is on efficiency: the authors train smaller models longer, noting that a 7B model keeps improving after 1T tokens [c749]. It is trained only on publicly available data [c750]. LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, and LLaMA-65B is competitive with Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B [c749]. The 65B model trained on 1.4T tokens over 2048 A100 GPUs in roughly 21 days [c762][c758].

**Llama 2 (2307.09288).** Llama 2 is a family of pretrained and fine-tuned models at 7B, 13B, and 70B parameters, trained between January and July 2023 [c1025][c815]. The chat variants (Llama 2-Chat) use supervised fine-tuning and RLHF for helpfulness and safety [c1025]. The paper places heavy emphasis on safety: fine-tuning reduces 70B toxicity from 24.60 to 0.01 and raises truthfulness from 50.18 to 64.14 [c916][c937]. The models are released under a custom commercial license [c1025].

**PaLM (2204.02311).** PaLM is a 540-billion-parameter, densely activated Transformer trained on 780 billion tokens using the Pathways system across 6144 TPU v4 chips [c3129][c3137]. Its emphasis is on scaling: it achieves state-of-the-art few-shot results on hundreds of tasks, and many BIG-bench tasks show discontinuous gains with scale [c3129]. The authors note that data begins to repeat in some subcorpora after 780B tokens, which is why training stopped there [c3299].

**Mistral 7B (2310.06825).** Mistral 7B is a 7-billion-parameter model built for efficiency. It uses grouped-query attention for faster inference and sliding window attention to handle long sequences at reduced cost [c2121]. The authors report it outperforms Llama 2 13B across all evaluated benchmarks [c2121][c2122]. Its advantage is strongest on reasoning, math, and code; on knowledge benchmarks it is only on par with Llama 2 13B, which the authors attribute to its smaller parameter count [c2133]. It is released under Apache 2.0 [c2121].

**Comparison.** The families differ mainly in their goals. GPT-3 and PaLM push raw scale (175B and 540B) to unlock few-shot ability. LLaMA trades parameter count for longer training on public data to reach strong performance at lower inference cost. Llama 2 adds chat alignment and safety work on top of open releases. Mistral 7B shows that architectural choices (GQA, SWA) let a 7B model beat a 13B one. Note that the library contains no direct benchmark comparison between GPT-3 and PaLM beyond what these papers report individually.

text:
**Research brief: Architectures for LLM-based agents (MemGPT, Generative Agents, AutoGen, HuggingGPT)**

**Memory**

*MemGPT.* MemGPT is inspired by virtual memory paging between physical memory and disk, providing the illusion of an extended context [c2289][c2290]. It separates main context (the LLM prompt tokens) from external context (information held outside the fixed context window) [c2295]. The LLM manages its own memory through function calls that move data between tiers, and it can chain these calls to perform multi-step retrieval [c2295][c2301]. MemGPT can write data to persistent memory after receiving a system alert about limited context space, and can search out-of-context data to bring relevant information into the current window [c2292].

*Generative Agents.* The memory stream is a long-term store of natural-language observations, each with a creation timestamp and a most recent access timestamp [c2358]. Retrieval scores memories by recency, importance, and relevance, and the top-ranked memories that fit the context window are included in the prompt [c2360][c2359]. Reflections are higher-level memories generated periodically when accumulated importance exceeds a threshold, and reflections can build on other reflections [c2363].

*AutoGen.* The retrieved passages do not describe a dedicated long-term memory module for AutoGen. Its retrieval-augmented variant uses a vector database as the context retriever for question answering and code generation [c2440][c2442].

*HuggingGPT.* Multi-turn context is handled through chat logs: the planning prompt includes previous chat logs so the controller can trace user-mentioned resources [c2586]. The retrieved passages do not describe a separate memory store beyond this.

**Planning**

*MemGPT.* The retrieved passages focus on context management rather than explicit task planning. Function chaining lets the processor execute multiple function calls sequentially before control returns to the user [c2301].

*Generative Agents.* Plans describe a future sequence of actions with a location, starting time, and duration, and they are stored in the memory stream and retrieved alongside observations and reflections [c2366]. The top-down process first creates a broad agenda and then recursively generates more detail [c2368]. Agents may change their plans midstream when reacting to observations [c2366].

*AutoGen.* The retrieved passages do not describe a separate planner. Control flow is conversation-driven: participating agents decide which agents to message and in what procedure, as functions of the inter-agent conversation [c2435].

*HuggingGPT.* Planning is an explicit stage in which the LLM parses the user request into a task list and determines execution order and resource dependencies [c2576]. Demonstrations in the prompt help the model understand task dependencies [c2586]. The authors note that global planning produces a full plan in one query but cannot guarantee correctness of each step, whereas iterative planning can enter an endless loop if one step errs [c2615].

**Coordination**

*MemGPT.* The LLM processor's outputs are parsed and executed by a function executor, and results are fed back to the processor [c2298]. Function calls also manage control flow between context management, response generation, and user interaction [c2290].

*Generative Agents.* Agents coordinate through a shared environment: a sandbox server updates object states from agent actions and sends each agent the agents and objects within its visual range [c2371].

*AutoGen.* Coordination is through multi-agent conversation. Agents share unified send/receive and generate-reply interfaces, and auto-reply drives the conversation unless a termination condition is met [c2436]. Dynamic group chat uses a GroupChatManager that selects a speaker, collects its response, and broadcasts it [c2447]. In a 12-task pilot, a role-play speaker-selection prompt yielded more successes and fewer LLM calls than a task-based prompt [c2501][c2502].

*HuggingGPT.* An LLM controller coordinates expert models. Candidate models are filtered by task type and ranked by downloads to fit the context limit [c2587]. Tasks with resource dependencies are executed in order, with results from prerequisite tasks injected into dependent ones [c2613]. The LLM then integrates the structured inference results into a response [c2590].

**Comparison**

MemGPT centres on managing a fixed context window through paging-style memory tiers and self-directed function calls [c2295][c2289]. Generative Agents use a retrieval-driven memory stream with reflection and planning inside a simulated world [c2358][c2363][c2366]. AutoGen centres coordination on conversation patterns among multiple agents [c2435][c2436]. HuggingGPT uses an LLM as a planner and dispatcher over external expert models [c2576][c2579]. The retrieved evidence describes these designs but does not include comparative benchmarks of memory quality across the four systems, so a head-to-head evaluation of memory cannot be drawn from the library.

# Research Brief: Architectures for LLM-Based Agents

## MemGPT (memory)
MemGPT is inspired by OS virtual memory: it augments a fixed-context LLM with a hierarchical memory system and functions that let the LLM manage its own memory [c2290][c2292]. Main context consists of the LLM prompt tokens, which can be accessed during inference, while external context refers to information held outside the fixed context window [c2295]. The prompt tokens are split into read-only system instructions, a fixed-size read/write working context, and a FIFO queue of recent messages [c2293]. Functions move data between main context and external context (archival and recall storage) [c2295]. When prompt tokens exceed a warning threshold, the queue manager inserts a memory-pressure warning; at a flush threshold it evicts messages and generates a recursive summary, while evicted messages remain stored in recall storage [c2297]. The LLM can chain function calls to perform multi-step retrieval [c2295][c2301].

## Generative Agents (memory, planning)
Generative Agents use a memory stream, a long-term record of the agent's experiences in natural language [c2326][c2358]. Retrieval combines relevance, recency, and importance, with all weights set to 1 in the implementation [c2360][c2359]. Importance is scored by directly asking the language model for an integer rating [c2360]. Reflection synthesizes higher-level inferences from memories; in the implementation, reflections are generated when the sum of importance scores for recent events exceeds a threshold of 150, and reflections are stored alongside observations [c2363]. Planning translates conclusions and the environment into high-level plans, recursively decomposed into finer-grained actions, and plans are saved in the memory stream [c2326][c2365]. Ablation results show reflection is required for deeper synthesis, as an agent without reflection could not answer a gift question as well [c2393].

## AutoGen (coordination)
AutoGen's core abstraction is the conversable agent, which can use LLMs, humans, tools, or a combination, and can receive, react to, and respond to messages [c2426][c2431]. Developers define agents and then program the interaction between them through conversation-centric computation and control [c2426][c2435]. Dynamic conversation flows can be achieved with customized reply functions or with LLM-driven function calls that message additional agents [c2437]. The GroupChatManager repeatedly selects a speaker, collects its response, and broadcasts the message to other agents [c2447]. A pilot study on 12 tasks found that a role-play speaker-selection prompt achieved a higher success rate and fewer LLM calls than a task-based prompt [c2501][c2502]. The retrieved passages do not describe a dedicated memory mechanism for AutoGen, nor a separate planning module.

## HuggingGPT (planning, coordination)
HuggingGPT uses an LLM as the controller across four stages: task planning, model selection, task execution, and response generation [c2576][c2580]. Task planning parses the request into a task list with execution order and resource dependencies, using slots for task, id, dependencies, and arguments [c2576][c2585]. Model selection uses expert-model descriptions from Hugging Face, filtering by task type and ranking by downloads to a top-K candidate set [c2587]. Expert models execute the assigned tasks, and the LLM integrates their structured results into a response [c2590]. HuggingGPT's global planning produces the full task queue in one query, which the paper contrasts with iterative step-by-step planning used by agents such as AutoGPT [c2615]. The retrieved passages do not describe a memory component for HuggingGPT.

## Comparison and Gaps
- **Memory:** MemGPT provides explicit tiered memory managed by the LLM through functions [c2295]; Generative Agents provide a scored memory stream with reflection [c2326][c2363]. The retrieved passages do not describe a memory mechanism for AutoGen or HuggingGPT.
- **Planning:** Generative Agents plan hierarchically, from high-level plans to detailed actions [c2326][c2365]; HuggingGPT plans globally in one query [c2615]. The retrieved passages do not describe a planning module for MemGPT or AutoGen.
- **Coordination:** AutoGen coordinates multiple conversing agents via group chat [c2447]; HuggingGPT coordinates expert models under a single LLM controller [c2576]. The retrieved passages describe MemGPT and Generative Agents primarily as single-agent architectures.

The library does not cover direct head-to-head benchmarks across all four systems.

**Research brief: What distinguishes GPT-3, LLaMA, Llama 2, PaLM and Mistral 7B**

**GPT-3.** GPT-3 is a 175B-parameter autoregressive model, and the paper's main contribution is testing in-context learning by evaluating it in few-shot, one-shot and zero-shot settings across more than two dozen NLP datasets [c572]. Its family spans 125M to 175B parameters, trained on 300B tokens each, with cross-entropy loss following a smooth power law with scale [c584][c583][c593]. Its emphasis is in-context learning rather than fine-tuning [c572]. On TriviaQA, the zero-shot result already beats fine-tuned T5-11B [c605].

**LLaMA.** LLaMA is a family from 7B to 65B parameters, trained on trillions of tokens using only publicly available datasets [c749]. Its emphasis is efficiency at inference: the authors argue a smaller model trained longer will ultimately be cheaper to run [c749]. LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, and LLaMA-65B is competitive with Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B [c749]. Training uses a BPE tokenizer that splits numbers into digits [c757].

**Llama 2.** Llama 2 is released at 7B, 13B and 70B parameters, with both pretrained and fine-tuned chat variants [c815][c1025]. Relative to Llama 1 it uses more robust data cleaning, about 40% more tokens, a doubled 4096-token context, and grouped-query attention in the larger models [c829][c832][c942]. Llama 2-Chat is tuned with supervised fine-tuning and RLHF, with a heavy emphasis on helpfulness and safety [c1025][c894]. The authors say it is competitive with some closed-source models but still lags GPT-4 [c937].

**PaLM.** PaLM is a 540B-parameter dense Transformer trained on 6144 TPU v4 chips using the Pathways system [c3129][c3128]. Its emphasis is scaling: it reports state-of-the-art few-shot results on hundreds of benchmarks, with breakthroughs on multi-step reasoning and BIG-bench, and many BIG-bench tasks show discontinuous gains with scale [c3129]. It also reports bias, toxicity and memorization analyses [c3129].

**Mistral 7B.** Mistral 7B is a 7B-parameter model that the authors claim outperforms Llama 2 13B on all benchmarks tested [c2122][c2131]. Its architectural distinctives are grouped-query attention and sliding window attention, which speed inference and handle longer sequences at reduced cost [c2122][c2125]. The emphasis is efficiency: it mirrors the performance of a Llama 2 model over three times its size on reasoning and MMLU [c2131].

**Comparison.** The families differ mainly in emphasis. GPT-3 studies in-context learning at a single large scale [c572]; LLaMA emphasises compute-efficient, publicly-sourced training across sizes [c749]; Llama 2 adds chat tuning and safety [c1025]; PaLM pushes raw scale and reasoning [c3129]; and Mistral 7B focuses on efficient architecture at small size [c2122]. The library does not contain a direct head-to-head benchmark across all five families, so cross-family performance comparisons beyond those cited are not supported here.

# Research Brief: BERT, RoBERTa, BART, and T5

## Architecture family
- **BERT**: Uses a bidirectional Transformer, so representations are conditioned on both left and right context in all layers [c390].
- **RoBERTa**: Matches the architecture and training objective of BERT-Large [c4372]; its contribution lies in pre-training recipe changes rather than architecture [c4370].
- **BART**: The decoder works left-to-right during pre-training, matching the setting during generation [c4340]. It is a sequence-to-sequence model that maps corrupted documents back to the originals [c4340].
- **T5**: The library passages do not describe T5's architecture in detail. Only passages on T5's pre-training objective and adaptation (below) are available. The T5 paper itself (1910.10683) is in the library but no passage from it was supplied, so I cannot cite its architecture.

## Pre-training objective
- **BERT**: Uses masked language modeling plus next sentence prediction [c390]. Masked prediction is slower to converge than a left-to-right model, but its empirical gains outweigh that cost [c390].
- **RoBERTa**: Same masked LM objective as BERT, but with dynamic masking, full-sentence inputs without NSP loss, large mini-batches, and a larger byte-level BPE vocabulary [c4370]. Pre-training on more data and for longer improves results [c4372].
- **BART**: Corrupted-document reconstruction with a left-to-right decoder [c4340]. The masked and permuted LM variants perform less well on generation, and BART adds left-to-right autoregressive pre-training [c4327].
- **T5**: Uses a "span corruption" objective by default. Per the Prompt Tuning analysis, this objective is poorly suited to training frozen models for later prompt conditioning; models trained to read and write sentinel tokens are hard to apply directly to plain text tasks [c4009].

## Adaptation to downstream tasks
- **BERT**: Two strategies exist: feature-based (task-specific architectures using pre-trained representations as features) and fine-tuning (minimal task-specific parameters, all pre-trained parameters fine-tuned) [c349]. BERT uses the fine-tuning approach, and the same pre-trained parameters initialize models for different downstream tasks [c358].
- **RoBERTa**: Adapted by fine-tuning on GLUE tasks; task-specific modifications are used for two GLUE tasks [c4376]. Parameter-efficient adaptation such as LoRA has been evaluated on RoBERTa base and large [c107].
- **BART**: The library passages describe BART's pre-training and generation performance but do not detail its fine-tuning procedure, so this cannot be fully cited.
- **T5**: Parameter-efficient prompt tuning freezes the model and tunes only prompt embeddings, reaching under 0.01% task-specific parameters for most sizes [c4009].

## Comparison and conclusion
BERT and RoBERTa share an encoder-only bidirectional architecture and MLM objective, with RoBERTa differing mainly in training recipe [c4370][c4372]. BART is a denoising sequence-to-sequence model with a left-to-right decoder, aimed at generation as well as discrimination [c4340][c4327]. T5 is not covered in enough detail by the supplied passages for a full comparison; its span-corruption objective and prompt-tuning behavior are the only T5-specific evidence available [c4009]. Gaps: T5 architecture and fine-tuning, and BART's fine-tuning procedure, are not covered by the supplied evidence.

I have enough evidence to compare the four models. One gap to flag: the library has no T5 span-corruption detail beyond what's cited, and I did not search for BERT's fine-tuning details beyond the passages returned.

**Architecture family**
- **BERT** uses a bidirectional Transformer (encoder-only), conditioned on both left and right context in all layers [c390].
- **RoBERTa** is a replication of BERT with the same architecture, retrained with changed recipe choices [c4341].
- **BART** uses a standard Transformer-based sequence-to-sequence architecture with a bidirectional encoder over corrupted text and a left-to-right autoregressive decoder [c4312].
- **T5** is an encoder-decoder Transformer; the authors found the original encoder-decoder form worked best, and it has about twice the parameters of encoder-only or decoder-only models at similar compute [c523].

**Pre-training objective**
- **BERT**: masked language modeling (Cloze-inspired), plus next sentence prediction (NSP) [c352].
- **RoBERTa**: same MLM objective, but with dynamic masking (new mask patterns each epoch instead of one static mask), full-sentence inputs without NSP, large mini-batches, and a larger byte-level BPE vocabulary [c4370][c4361]. Its authors found BERT was significantly undertrained [c4341].
- **BART**: a denoising autoencoder that corrupts text with an arbitrary noising function and reconstructs the original with cross-entropy loss; the best noising combined sentence shuffling and span in-filling [c4306][c4312].
- **T5**: text-to-text framing of all tasks; the unsupervised objective is denoising, and the authors suggest objectives with short target sequences for efficiency [c523]. Their comparison included prefix LM, BERT-style MLM, and deshuffling [c465].

**Downstream adaptation**
- **BERT**: fine-tuning approach (all parameters updated), as opposed to feature-based ELMo [c390].
- **RoBERTa**: the library's passages describe its pre-training changes; they do not detail a separate downstream adaptation method, so I have no cited evidence for one.
- **BART**: for classification, the same input is fed to encoder and decoder and the final decoder representation is used; for generation, the decoder is fine-tuned directly; for translation, a small new encoder replaces the embeddings [c4320].
- **T5**: every task uses the same model, loss, and decoding, with short task prefixes (e.g., "translate English to German:") [c407][c426]. Fine-tuning is done per task, not multi-task [c426]. The paper also studies parameter-subset fine-tuning alternatives for low-resource settings [c488].

**Comparison**: BERT and RoBERTa are encoder-only and share an MLM objective, with RoBERTa differing mainly in training recipe. BART and T5 are encoder-decoder denoising models; BART is the closer analogue to BERT's bidirectional encoder plus a GPT-style decoder [c4304], while T5 unifies all tasks as text generation.

- **BERT**: masked language modeling (Cloze-inspired), plus next sentence prediction (NSP) [c352].

- **RoBERTa**: same MLM objective, but with dynamic masking (new mask patterns each epoch instead of one static mask), full-sentence inputs without NSP, large mini-batches, and a larger byte-level BPE vocabulary [c4370][c4361].
Its authors found BERT was significantly undertrained [c4341].

- **BART**: a denoising autoencoder that corrupts text with an arbitrary noising function and reconstructs the original with cross-entropy loss; the best noising combined sentence shuffling and span in-filling [c4306][c4312].
- **T5**: text-to-text framing of all tasks; the unsupervised objective is denoising, and the authors suggest objectives with short target sequences for efficiency [c523].
Their comparison included prefix LM, BERT-style MLM, and deshuffling [c465].
- **BERT**: fine-tuning approach (all parameters updated), as opposed to feature-based ELMo [c390].
- **RoBERTa**: the library's passages describe its pre-training changes; they do not detail a separate downstream adaptation method, so I have no cited evidence for one.

- **BART**: for classification, the same input is fed to encoder and decoder and the final decoder representation is used; for generation, the decoder is fine-tuned directly; for translation, a small new encoder replaces the embeddings [c4320].
- **T5**: every task uses the same model, loss, and decoding, with short task prefixes (e.g., "translate English to German:") [c407][c426].
Fine-tuning is done per task, not multi-task [c426].
The paper also studies parameter-subset fine-tuning alternatives for low-resource settings [c488].
**Comparison**: BERT and RoBERTa are encoder-only and share an MLM objective, with RoBERTa differing mainly in training recipe.
BART and T5 are encoder-decoder denoising models; BART is the closer analogue to BERT's bidirectional encoder plus a GPT-style decoder [c4304], while T5 unifies all tasks as text generation.

text:
**Research brief: distinguishing GPT-3, LLaMA, Llama 2, PaLM and Mistral 7B**

**GPT-3.** GPT-3 is a 175B-parameter autoregressive model whose main contribution is the study of in-context learning: it is evaluated under zero-, one- and few-shot conditions with no gradient updates [c572][c573]. Smaller models (125M to 13B parameters) were trained to compare their performance against it [c576].

**LLaMA.** LLaMA is a family from 7B to 65B parameters, trained on trillions of tokens using only publicly available datasets [c749][c750]. Its emphasis is efficient performance at a given inference budget, with smaller models trained on more tokens [c750]. LLaMA-13B reportedly outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, and LLaMA-65B is competitive with Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B [c749][c793].

**Llama 2.** Llama 2 spans 7B to 70B parameters, with pretrained and chat-tuned variants [c815][c1025]. Compared with Llama 1 it uses more robust data cleaning, about 40% more training tokens, a doubled context length (4096), and grouped-query attention in the larger models [c829][c832][c942]. Its distinctive emphasis is dialogue use and safety: Llama 2-Chat is tuned with supervised fine-tuning and RLHF to align with human preferences for helpfulness and safety [c1025][c894].

**PaLM.** PaLM is a dense 540B-parameter Transformer trained on 6144 TPU v4 chips using the Pathways system, on 780B tokens [c3128][c3137][c3138]. Its emphasis is scaling and breadth: state-of-the-art few-shot results across many benchmarks, with a significant number of BIG-bench tasks showing discontinuous improvements from model scale [c3129]. The paper reports estimated training emissions of 271.43 tCO2e for PaLM-540B [c3314].

**Mistral 7B.** Mistral 7B is a 7B-parameter model that the authors report outperforms Llama 2 13B across all evaluated benchmarks [c2121][c2131]. It uses grouped-query attention and sliding window attention, the latter to handle longer sequences at reduced computational cost [c2121][c2125]. Its emphasis is on efficiency: it is presented as delivering high performance while maintaining efficient inference [c2122].

**Comparison.** The evidence supports only a partial contrast. GPT-3 is the source of the few-shot in-context learning framing at 175B [c572]; PaLM is the largest dense model here at 540B [c3128]; LLaMA and Mistral 7B are both presented as efficiency-oriented, with LLaMA trained on publicly available data only [c749][c2122]; Llama 2 is presented for dialogue and safety [c1025]. The library does not provide a direct head-to-head evaluation of all five models, and it does not give a basis for comparing Llama 2's performance against GPT-4 beyond the paper's own statement, so comparative claims are limited to what each paper reports.

text:
**GPT-3 (2005.14165).** Main contribution: showing that a very large autoregressive model can perform tasks via in-context learning, in zero-, one-, and few-shot settings with no gradient updates [c572][c573]. Scale: 175B parameters, with smaller models from 125M to 13B trained for comparison [c576][c584]. Training emphasis: scaling model size and data, with all models trained for 300B tokens [c583]. In the few-shot setting, performance gains grow with model capacity [c576][c605].

**LLaMA (2302.13971).** Main contribution: a family of foundation models trained exclusively on publicly available datasets [c749][c750]. Scale: 7B to 65B parameters [c749]. Training emphasis: the paper trains on trillions of tokens, and the authors note the 7B model's performance continued to improve even after 1T tokens [c749]. LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks [c749].

**Llama 2 (2307.09288).** Main contribution: open pretrained and fine-tuned models, with Llama 2-Chat optimized for dialogue, and a detailed account of safety-focused fine-tuning [c814][c825][c894]. Scale: 7B to 70B parameters [c825]. Training emphasis: pretraining on 2T tokens, with the context window expanded from 2048 to 4096 tokens [c833][c942]; grouped-query attention is used in the larger models [c832]. Safety tuning combined supervised fine-tuning with RLHF using safety data [c894][c896].

**PaLM (2204.02311).** Main contribution: a 540B-parameter model trained with the Pathways system across two TPU v4 pods, with state-of-the-art few-shot results on many tasks [c3128][c3129][c3138]. Scale: 540B dense parameters, with 8B and 62B variants [c3328]. Training emphasis: a 780B-token pretraining corpus mixing filtered webpages, books, Wikipedia, news articles, source code, and social media conversations, trained on exactly one epoch [c3150]. The paper reports high training throughput and utilization for the 540B model [c3160].

**Mistral 7B (2310.06825).** Main contribution: a 7B model that outperforms Llama 2 13B across all evaluated benchmarks, using grouped-query attention and sliding window attention for efficient inference [c2122][c2131]. Scale: 7B parameters [c2121]. Training emphasis: the library's evidence centres on architecture and efficiency rather than training data. A fine-tuned chat variant, Mistral 7B – Instruct, is also released and outperforms all 7B models on MT-Bench [c2132].

**Comparison.** The families differ mainly in emphasis: GPT-3 established in-context learning at 175B scale [c572]; LLaMA and Mistral 7B both target strong performance at small sizes, with LLaMA trained on public data only [c749][c2122]; Llama 2 adds open chat models with safety work [c814][c894]; PaLM pushes the largest dense scale and training infrastructure [c3128][c3129]. The library does not contain a direct benchmark comparison across all five families, so cross-family performance rankings beyond the pairwise claims above are not established here.

text:
**Research brief: BERT, RoBERTa, BART, and T5**

**1. Architecture family**
- BERT is a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder, with BERTBASE (L=12, H=768, A=12) and BERTLARGE (L=24, H=1024, A=16) [c360][c359].
- RoBERTa uses the same architecture and training objective as BERTLARGE [c4372][c4376]; its changes are in the training recipe, not the model structure.
- BART is a sequence-to-sequence model with a bidirectional encoder over corrupted text and a left-to-right autoregressive decoder [c4312]. It uses a standard Transformer NMT architecture [c4306].
- T5 casts all tasks as text-to-text and uses the original encoder-decoder Transformer form, which the authors found worked best [c523].

**2. Pre-training objective**
- BERT uses a masked language model (MLM) that predicts randomly masked tokens from bidirectional context [c351][c352], plus a binarized next sentence prediction (NSP) task [c366].
- RoBERTa keeps the MLM objective but uses dynamic masking (a new mask pattern each time a sequence is fed), drops NSP, uses full-sentence inputs, larger mini-batches, and a larger byte-level BPE vocabulary [c4370][c4362][c4366]. It is trained on more data and for longer [c4341][c4372].
- BART is trained by corrupting documents with an arbitrary noising function and reconstructing the original text [c4305][c4304]. The best-performing noise combines sentence permutation with a text-infilling scheme in which spans (length drawn from a Poisson distribution, λ = 3) are replaced by a single mask token [c4315][c4326].
- T5 uses a span-corruption denoising objective: about 15% of tokens are dropped, consecutive spans are replaced by unique sentinel tokens, and the target reconstructs the dropped spans [c442][c441]. The authors found that most denoising variants performed similarly, and they recommend objectives with short targets for efficiency [c523][c471].

**3. Adaptation to downstream tasks**
- BERT is fine-tuned: all parameters are initialized from pre-training and jointly fine-tuned, with one added output layer per task [c358][c367]. A feature-based alternative (fixed features from a frozen model) is also evaluated [c384].
- RoBERTa is fine-tuned in the same manner as BERT, with task-specific adjustments for some GLUE tasks such as the QNLI ranking formulation [c4376]. The library does not describe its fine-tuning procedure in further detail.
- BART is fine-tuned as a sequence-to-sequence model for generation tasks such as abstractive QA and summarization. For classification, the same input is fed to the encoder and decoder and the final decoder representation is used [c4320]. For machine translation, a new encoder is learned to replace the word embeddings [c4313][c4320].
- T5 casts every task as text-to-text by adding a task-specific text prefix to the input (e.g., "translate English to German:"), and trains with a maximum-likelihood objective regardless of task [c424]. Classification outputs a label word; Winograd-style tasks are reformulated by highlighting the ambiguous pronoun [c428].

**Comparison and conclusion**
BERT and RoBERTa share an encoder-only architecture and MLM objective, differing mainly in training recipe (RoBERTa drops NSP and trains longer on more data). BART and T5 both use encoder-decoder models with denoising objectives, but BART emphasizes flexible corruption (including infilling and permutation), while T5 standardizes all tasks into a single text-to-text format with a span-corruption objective. All four are adapted by fine-tuning on labeled data; the sequence-to-sequence models (BART, T5) do so by generating target text.

**Gaps:** The library does not contain details on RoBERTa's fine-tuning beyond the GLUE notes above, nor a direct head-to-head comparison of all four models on the same benchmark.

text:
**Research brief: LoRA vs. QLoRA and memory savings for a 65B model**

**How LoRA and QLoRA relate**

QLoRA is an efficient finetuning approach that backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters (LoRA) [c277]. In other words, it builds on LoRA: the base model is quantized to 4-bit precision and LoRA adapters are trained on top [c284]. The paper describes its contribution as a better-tuned LoRA approach that includes adapters at every network layer, which avoids almost all of the accuracy tradeoffs seen in prior work [c281].

QLoRA adds three innovations to reduce memory without sacrificing performance: (1) 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), a data type described as information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed data; (2) Double Quantization, which quantizes the quantization constants; and (3) Paged Optimizers, which use NVIDIA unified memory to avoid gradient-checkpointing memory spikes on long sequences [c281].

**Memory savings for a 65B model**

QLoRA reduces the average memory requirement of finetuning a 65B parameter model from >780GB of GPU memory to <48GB, without degrading runtime or predictive performance relative to a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline [c280]. Double Quantization alone saves about 0.37 bits per parameter, approximately 3 GB for a 65B model [c281].

**Empirical support and limitations**

On MMLU, NF4 with double quantization fully recovers 16-bit LoRA performance for LLaMA 7B through 65B, while QLoRA with FP4 lags the 16-bit LoRA baseline by about one percentage point [c301]. The authors note, however, that they did not establish that QLoRA matches full 16-bit finetuning at 33B and 65B scales due to resource costs, leaving this to future work [c329].
