# Research Brief: Token Order, Sequence Length, and Long-Context Use

## 1. Original Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017)

**Token order.** The model contains no recurrence and no convolution, so information about the order of the sequence must be injected. Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks [c15]. The authors use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies, with each dimension corresponding to a sinusoid [c15]. Learned positional embeddings were also tried and produced nearly identical results; the sinusoidal version was chosen because it may allow extrapolation to sequence lengths longer than those encountered during training [c15].

**Sequence length.** Self-attention connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires O(n) sequential operations [c16]. Self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when sequence length is smaller than the representation dimensionality, which is most often the case for sentence representations used in machine translation [c16][c17]. Restricting self-attention to a neighborhood of size r would increase the maximum path length to O(n/r); the authors plan to investigate this in future work [c17].

## 2. RoPE (Su et al., RoFormer, 2021)

**Token order.** Earlier approaches typically add position information to the context representations, either as a pre-defined sinusoidal encoding or as trainable absolute embeddings [c2148][c2144]. RoPE instead encodes the absolute position with a rotation matrix and incorporates explicit relative position dependency in the self-attention formulation [c2142][c2145]. Rather than adding position terms, it multiplies the context representations by a rotation matrix, so relative position is captured through the rotation matrix product [c2155].

**Sequence length.** RoPE is claimed to offer sequence length flexibility and a decaying inter-token dependency as relative distance increases [c2145][c2142]. The authors pre-trained on approximately 34GB of Chinese data and report that accuracy rises with an increasing upper bound on sequence length, which they attribute to the generalizability of RoPE [c2183]. The library does not contain further quantitative length-extrapolation results for RoPE.

## 3. Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023)

**Token order and content.** Mamba is built on structured state space models and has no attention or MLP blocks [c4191]. Its key change is letting the SSM parameters be functions of the input, so the model can selectively propagate or forget information along the sequence depending on the current token [c4191]. The paper identifies content-based reasoning as a key weakness of prior subquadratic models, which this selection mechanism is designed to address [c4191].

**Sequence length.** Input-dependent parameters rule out convolutions, so the authors use a hardware-aware parallel algorithm in recurrent mode [c4191]. The resulting implementation scales linearly in sequence length, compared with pseudo-linear scaling for convolution-based SSMs [c4195]. Mamba enjoys 5× higher inference throughput than Transformers and linear scaling in sequence length [c4191]. On a selective copying-style task it generalizes perfectly to million-length sequences, about 4000× longer than seen in training, while no other method in that comparison goes beyond 2× [c4232]. In DNA pretraining, Mamba's perplexity improves as context grows up to 1M tokens, whereas HyenaDNA gets worse with sequence length [c4242].

## 4. "Lost in the Middle" (Liu et al., 2023)

Performance depends on where relevant information sits within a long input. Across multi-document QA and key-value retrieval, performance is highest when relevant information occurs at the beginning or end of the context and degrades significantly when models must use information in the middle, even for explicitly long-context models [c2775][c2781]. This produces a U-shaped curve reflecting primacy and recency biases [c2775]. For GPT-3.5-Turbo, multi-document QA performance can drop by more than 20%; in the 20- and 30-document settings it falls below closed-book performance [c2790]. GPT-4 achieves the highest absolute performance among the models evaluated but still shows a U-shaped curve [c2821][c2822]. Encoder-decoder models are relatively robust to position within their training-time sequence length, but show the U-shape when evaluated on longer sequences [c2780].

## Comparison and Conclusion

The three approaches differ in how they handle order. The original Transformer adds fixed sinusoidal (or learned) position encodings to its inputs [c15]. RoPE rotates the context representations to encode relative position inside self-attention [c2155]. Mamba drops explicit position encodings and relies on a recurrent state with input-dependent selection [c4191]. On cost, the original Transformer's self-attention needs constant sequential operations but grows with sequence length in the way described above [c16], while Mamba is reported as linear in length with higher inference throughput [c4191]; the library does not give a direct cost comparison between RoPE and the others.

"Lost in the Middle" shows that a long context window alone does not guarantee that information in the middle of the input will be used [c2775][c2781]. The library documents this for the decoder-only and encoder-decoder language models it tested, including the Transformer-based models studied there [c2801][c2780]. It does not test RoPE-based or Mamba models on this task, so the library does not establish whether those architectures show the same effect.

# Research Brief: Architectures for LLM-Based Agents

## MemGPT (memory and control flow)
MemGPT is an OS-inspired system that provides the illusion of an unbounded context by managing a hierarchy of memory tiers [c2289][c2290]. Its main context consists of the LLM prompt tokens, while external context is held outside the fixed context window [c2295]. The prompt tokens are split into system instructions, a working context, and a FIFO queue [c2293]. When prompt tokens approach the context limit, the queue manager warns the LLM so it can store important information via function calls [c2297]. Multi-step operation is supported by function chaining, which lets the LLM request immediate follow-up inference [c2295][c2301].

## Generative Agents (memory, planning, reflection)
The architecture has three components: a memory stream recording experiences in natural language, reflection that synthesizes memories into higher-level inferences, and planning that turns conclusions into action plans [c2326]. Memory objects store a description and timestamps [c2358]. Retrieval scores memories by recency, importance, and relevance, combined with equal weights [c2359][c2360]. Reflection is triggered when accumulated importance exceeds a threshold and produces trees of higher-level thoughts [c2363]. Planning begins with a broad daily agenda and is recursively decomposed into finer-grained actions [c2368][c2365]. Plans are stored in the memory stream and included in retrieval [c2366].

## AutoGen (coordination and memory)
AutoGen is a multi-agent conversation framework built on customizable, conversable agents that can use LLMs, humans, or tools [c2426][c2430]. Its coordination model, conversation programming, defines computation (agent actions) and control flow (conversation-driven sequencing) [c2435]. Dynamic flows can be implemented through custom reply functions or LLM-decided function calls [c2437]. The GroupChatManager dynamically selects a speaker, collects its response, and broadcasts it to others [c2447]. In the OptiGuide application, the Commander agent handles memory tied to user interactions and shares it across the system [c2494]. The retrieved passages do not describe a tiered long-term memory module comparable to MemGPT's.

## HuggingGPT (planning and coordination)
HuggingGPT uses an LLM as controller with four stages: task planning, model selection, task execution, and response generation [c2576][c2580]. Planning is global, producing the full task queue within one query, with dependencies represented through a `<resource>` symbol [c2615][c2588]. Demonstrations and chat logs in the prompt help with dependency resolution and multi-turn context [c2586]. Models are selected based on their Hugging Face descriptions [c2579]. The retrieved passages do not describe a memory mechanism beyond chat logs.

## Comparison
- **Memory:** MemGPT manages explicit tiered memory through function calls [c2295][c2297]; Generative Agents use a scored, reflective memory stream [c2326][c2359]; AutoGen's Commander holds user-interaction memory shared across agents [c2494]; HuggingGPT uses chat logs in its prompts [c2586].
- **Planning:** Generative Agents plan hierarchically from day to minute [c2368]; HuggingGPT plans globally in one query [c2615]; MemGPT's control flow is driven by function chaining rather than a planning module [c2301].
- **Coordination:** AutoGen coordinates multiple conversing agents [c2435][c2447]; HuggingGPT coordinates expert models under one LLM controller [c2580]; MemGPT and Generative Agents center on a single agent.

**Gap:** The library provides limited detail on AutoGen and HuggingGPT memory mechanisms beyond the cited passages, so claims about those are restricted to what is shown.

**Research brief: distinguishing GPT-3, LLaMA, Llama 2, PaLM and Mistral 7B**

**GPT-3.** GPT-3 is a 175B-parameter autoregressive model, and its main contribution is the study of in-context learning, evaluated in zero-, one- and few-shot settings across more than two dozen NLP datasets [c572]. It was trained on 300B tokens, with datasets weighted by quality rather than size, so CommonCrawl and Books2 were seen less than once [c587][c588]. The paper also reports a family of smaller models from 125M to 13B parameters for comparison [c576].

**LLaMA.** LLaMA is a family of models from 7B to 65B parameters, trained on trillions of tokens using only publicly available data [c749][c750]. Its emphasis is inference efficiency: the authors argue a smaller model trained longer is cheaper at inference, and LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks [c749]. The 65B model is trained on 1.4T tokens [c758][c762].

**Llama 2.** Llama 2 is a family of pretrained and fine-tuned models from 7B to 70B parameters, with Llama 2-Chat optimized for dialogue [c815]. Relative to Llama 1 it uses 40% more pretraining tokens, a 4096-token context and grouped-query attention for the larger models [c829][c832][c942]. Its distinctive emphasis is safety and alignment via supervised fine-tuning and RLHF, and it is released for commercial and research use [c1025][c841][c825].

**PaLM.** PaLM is a dense 540B-parameter Transformer trained on 780B tokens using the Pathways system across TPU v4 pods [c3129][c3137]. Its headline contribution is few-shot performance at scale, including breakthrough results on multi-step reasoning and BIG-bench [c3129]. The data mixture covers webpages, books, Wikipedia, news, code and conversations [c3150]. The paper also reports smaller 8B and 62B variants [c3328].

**Mistral 7B.** Mistral 7B is a 7B-parameter model that outperforms Llama 2 13B on all tested benchmarks [c2121][c2131]. It introduces grouped-query attention and sliding window attention to reduce inference cost [c2122][c2125], and is released under Apache 2.0 [c2123].

**Comparison.** The library supports only a partial contrast. GPT-3 is centred on in-context learning at 175B [c572]; LLaMA on training smaller models longer on public data [c749][c750]; Llama 2 on chat models with safety alignment [c815][c841]; PaLM on large-scale few-shot capability [c3129]; and Mistral 7B on attention-based inference efficiency at 7B [c2122]. The retrieved passages contain no direct head-to-head benchmark across all five families, so cross-family performance claims should be treated with caution.

**Research brief: LoRA and QLoRA**

**1. How LoRA and QLoRA relate**

LoRA freezes the pretrained model weights and injects trainable low-rank decomposition matrices into Transformer layers, so only the small matrices are trained [c82][c94]. The update is parameterized as W0 + ∆W = W0 + BA with rank r much smaller than the weight dimensions, and W0 receives no gradient updates [c94]. In most experiments LoRA was applied only to the attention weights Wq and Wv [c106]. It can match or beat full fine-tuning on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2 and GPT-3 while having fewer trainable parameters and no additional inference latency [c82][c85].

QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters [c277][c278]. Its main innovations are 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), Double Quantization, and Paged Optimizers [c281]. Whenever a QLoRA weight tensor is used, it is dequantized to BFloat16 for the matrix multiplication, and only the LoRA parameters receive weight gradients [c289][c294]. The QLoRA authors describe their method as a better-tuned LoRA approach that includes adapters at every network layer [c281].

**2. Memory savings for finetuning a 65B model**

The QLoRA paper reports that it reduces the average memory requirement for finetuning a 65B parameter model from over 780 GB of GPU memory to under 48 GB, without degrading runtime or predictive performance compared to a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline [c280]. This is what allows finetuning a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU [c277]. The paper also reports that 4-bit NF4 with double quantization fully recovers 16-bit LoRA MMLU performance on LLaMA 7B through 65B [c301], though it did not establish full 16-bit finetuning parity at the 33B and 65B scales due to resource costs [c329].

**3. Caveats**

The library's LoRA evidence is drawn from RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2 and GPT-3 experiments [c82][c100]; it does not cover LoRA behaviour at QLoRA's 33B and 65B scales. The 65B memory figure is the QLoRA paper's own reported measurement, and the provided passages contain no independent verification of it.

sentence_verdicts.text: LoRA freezes the pretrained model weights and injects trainable low-rank decomposition matrices into Transformer layers, so only the small matrices are trained [c82][c94].
The update is parameterized as W0 + ∆W = W0 + BA with rank r much smaller than the weight dimensions, and W0 receives no gradient updates [c94].
In most experiments LoRA was applied only to the attention weights Wq and Wv [c106].
It can match or beat full fine-tuning on RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2 and GPT-3 while having fewer trainable parameters and no additional inference latency [c82][c85].
QLoRA backpropagates gradients through a frozen, 4-bit quantized pretrained language model into Low Rank Adapters [c277][c278].
Its main innovations are 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4), Double Quantization, and Paged Optimizers [c281].
Whenever a QLoRA weight tensor is used, it is dequantized to BFloat16 for the matrix multiplication, and only the LoRA parameters receive weight gradients [c289][c294].
The QLoRA authors describe their method as a better-tuned LoRA approach that includes adapters at every network layer [c281].

The QLoRA paper reports that it reduces the average memory requirement for finetuning a 65B parameter model from over 780 GB of GPU memory to under 48 GB, without degrading runtime or predictive performance compared to a 16-bit fully finetuned baseline [c280].
This is what allows finetuning a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU [c277].

The paper also reports that 4-bit NF4 with double quantization fully recovers 16-bit LoRA MMLU performance on LLaMA 7B through 65B [c301], though it did not establish full 16-bit finetuning parity at the 33B and 65B scales due to resource costs [c329].
The library's LoRA evidence is drawn from RoBERTa, DeBERTa, GPT-2 and GPT-3 experiments [c82][c100]; it does not cover LoRA behaviour at QLoRA's 33B and 65B scales.
The 65B memory figure is the QLoRA paper's own reported measurement, and the provided passages contain no independent verification of it.

**Research brief: BERT, RoBERTa, BART and T5**

**Architecture family**
- BERT uses a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer encoder, based on the original Transformer implementation [c359]. Only BERT representations are jointly conditioned on both left and right context in all layers, unlike ELMo or OpenAI GPT [c390].
- RoBERTa is a replication study of BERT pretraining; it is trained with the same masked language modeling objective and architecture as BERTLARGE [c4376].
- BART is a denoising autoencoder implemented as a sequence-to-sequence model with a bidirectional encoder over corrupted text and a left-to-right autoregressive decoder [c4312][c4309]. It uses a standard Transformer-based neural machine translation architecture [c4306].
- T5 uses a standard encoder-decoder Transformer [c433] and casts every task into a text-to-text format [c424].

**Pre-training objective**
- BERT uses a masked language model objective and a "next sentence prediction" task [c352]. Sentence pairs are packed into one sequence with [CLS] and [SEP] tokens [c363].
- RoBERTa keeps the masked language modeling objective but changes the recipe: dynamic masking, FULL-SENTENCES without NSP loss, large mini-batches and a larger byte-level BPE [c4370]. Its authors find that BERT was significantly undertrained [c4341].
- BART is trained by corrupting text with an arbitrary noising function and learning to reconstruct the original text [c4306]. The authors find the best performance from shuffling the order of original sentences and a span in-filling scheme [c4306].
- T5 uses a span-corruption objective: randomly dropped-out spans of input tokens are each replaced with a sentinel token, and the target is the dropped-out spans delimited by those sentinels [c442][c441]. Variants of the BERT-style objective performed similarly in the authors' comparison [c469].

**Adaptation to downstream tasks**
- BERT is fine-tuned by adding a single output layer and jointly fine-tuning all parameters [c349][c358]. A feature-based alternative, using fixed features from the pre-trained model, is also evaluated [c384].
- RoBERTa is fine-tuned separately on each GLUE task with a limited hyperparameter sweep, using only that task's training data [c4374].
- BART can be fine-tuned as a standard sequence-to-sequence model for generation tasks [c4331]. For classification, the same input is fed to the encoder and decoder and the final decoder representation is used [c4320]. For machine translation, a new randomly initialized encoder replaces the input embeddings [c4316].
- T5 is fine-tuned on each task individually, with a short task prefix added to the input [c426]. The paper also evaluates multi-task training mixtures and other fine-tuning schemes [c492][c490].

**Comparison**
BERT and RoBERTa are both encoder-only bidirectional models, and RoBERTa changes mainly the training recipe rather than the architecture [c4376][c4370]. BART and T5 are encoder-decoder models; BART's denoising pretraining is applied to both generation and comprehension tasks [c4306], while T5 unifies all tasks into a single text-to-text format and training objective [c424].

**Gaps:** The library does not contain a direct head-to-head benchmark comparing all four models, and it does not give exact parameter counts for each model.

# Research Brief: Techniques for Handling Information Beyond the Context Window

## MemGPT (arXiv 2310.08560)
MemGPT borrows from OS virtual memory: it pages data between a fixed-context main memory and external storage, letting the LLM manage its own memory [c2289][c2290]. Its architecture has main context (prompt tokens) and external context outside the window, with functions that move data between them and a queue manager and function executor handling the flow [c2295]. The LLM can chain function calls via a heartbeat mechanism to perform multi-step retrieval [c2295]. The paper reports applications to document analysis, where documents far exceed the window, and multi-session chat, where agents retain memory over long interactions [c2289][c2318].

## RAPTOR (arXiv 2401.18059)
RAPTOR recursively embeds, clusters, and summarizes text chunks, building a tree bottom-up with summaries at increasing levels of abstraction [c4128][c4131]. Clustering is soft, so a node can belong to multiple clusters [c4138]. At query time, the paper compares tree traversal with collapsed-tree retrieval and finds the collapsed tree (flattening all layers and retrieving up to a token budget, about 2000 tokens) performs better on the QASPER subset [c4142][c4144][c4145]. Retrieval is at multiple granularities, and the paper reports state-of-the-art QA results, including with GPT-4 on QuALITY [c4128]. An ablation shows clustering beats a recency-based tree (56.6% vs 55.8%) [c4164].

## RETRO (arXiv 2112.04426)
RETRO conditions autoregressive generation on chunks retrieved from a large external database, using a frozen BERT-based key embedding for retrieval and a chunked cross-attention mechanism to integrate the retrieved neighbours [c3353][c3358][c3367]. It retrieves at chunk level rather than token level, which makes storage and computation feasible at trillion-token scale (kNN-LM would need about 15 TB for Wikipedia, versus 215 GB for RETRO) [c3389][c3358]. Retrieval can repeat during generation, since each chunk can trigger new neighbours [c3379][c3370]. Existing models can also be retrofitted by training only the new cross-attention and encoder weights, using about 3% of pre-training tokens [c3389][c3391].

## Lost in the Middle (arXiv 2307.03172)
This paper studies how well language models use long contexts rather than proposing a new technique. It shows that language models do not use long contexts robustly: performance is highest when relevant information is at the start or end of the input and drops when it sits in the middle, a U-shaped curve that holds across models [c2775][c2781]. The authors also report that query-aware contextualization (placing the query before and after the documents) greatly improves key-value retrieval but barely changes multi-document QA [c2805][c2804]. The U-shape persists even for GPT-4 and in base models without instruction tuning [c2822][c2781].

## Comparison and Conclusion
The approaches differ in mechanism. MemGPT manages context dynamically through paging and function calls [c2295]. RAPTOR and RETRO extend effective access through retrieval, RAPTOR over summary trees and RETRO over chunked external stores [c4128][c3353]. Lost in the Middle shows that even with a long window, placement of relevant information matters, which is a limitation that retrieval and paging strategies must account for [c2775]. The library does not contain evidence on how these methods compare head-to-head on a common benchmark.

**Research brief: DPO vs. PPO-based RLHF**

**What DPO's loss is.** None of the supplied evidence passages describe Direct Preference Optimization or give its loss function. The library therefore cannot answer this part of the task from its contents.

**What the evidence says about PPO-based RLHF.** The passages describe the standard pipeline: a reward model is trained on human comparisons with a cross-entropy loss, where the difference in rewards represents the log odds that one response is preferred [c1138][c1142]. The policy is then optimized against that reward with PPO, plus a per-token KL penalty from the SFT model to mitigate overoptimization of the reward model [c1144]. InstructGPT additionally mixes pretraining gradients into PPO to reduce regressions on public NLP datasets [c1119][c1220].

**Practical limitations of the PPO pipeline reported in the evidence.**
- Reward overoptimization and sensitivity: the KL penalty is used to mitigate overoptimization of the reward model [c1144], and the Anthropic HH work reports that PPO training required hyperparameter scans and is sensitive to settings [c4413][c3661].
- Compute and instability: using a 175B reward model and value function "greatly increase[s] the compute requirements of PPO," and larger RMs were less stable [c1215].
- Alignment tax: without mixing in pretraining updates, PPO models show performance regressions on public NLP datasets [c1232][c1174].
- Reward-model dependence: the reward function is itself learned, and the policy can exploit its weaknesses, so a KL penalty is used to reduce reward hacking [c864].

**Comparison.** The evidence supports the narrower claim that PPO-based RLHF involves several sensitive components (reward model, value function, KL coefficient, pretraining mix) and is compute-intensive at larger model sizes [c1215][c1144]. It does not contain a direct comparison with DPO, so any claimed advantage of DPO over PPO cannot be verified from this library. A proper answer would require sources describing DPO itself, which are not present here.

**Research brief: extra inference-time computation in chain-of-thought (CoT), self-consistency, and Tree of Thoughts (ToT)**

**Chain-of-thought prompting.** CoT elicits intermediate natural-language reasoning steps via few-shot exemplars, which lets a model allocate more computation to harder problems [c1269][c1262]. The authors ablated this: a variant emitting only dots equal to the equation length (variable compute without reasoning) performed about the same as the baseline, suggesting that the benefit comes from expressing intermediate steps in language rather than from extra tokens alone [c1283].

**Self-consistency (CoT-SC).** Rather than greedily decoding one reasoning path, self-consistency samples a diverse set of reasoning paths and takes a majority vote over final answers [c1380][c1386]. The authors report that performance rises with more sampled paths, and that in practice a small number (e.g., 5 or 10) can realize most of the gains while limiting cost [c1421][c1401]. It outperforms beam search under matched numbers of paths, because beam search yields less output diversity [c1408]. Self-consistency also improved GSM8K accuracy over greedy decoding on PaLM-540B, reaching 74.4% [c1432].

**Tree of Thoughts.** ToT treats problem solving as search over a tree whose nodes are partial solutions, with the LM generating candidate next "thoughts," evaluating states, and running search (BFS or DFS) with lookahead and backtracking [c1576][c1582][c1583]. Unlike CoT-SC, which votes over complete chains and has no local exploration within a chain [c1580], ToT explores alternative intermediate steps and can prune or backtrack [c1588]. On Game of 24, ToT achieved a 74% success rate, versus 4% for GPT-4 with CoT [c1573][c1597].

**Cost trade-off.** ToT is substantially more expensive: in Game of 24 it needed about 5.5k completion tokens per problem, close to 100 CoT trials, yet still outperformed the best of 100 independent CoT samples [c1626]. The authors describe cost as highly dependent on prompts and search algorithms, potentially 5–100 times more generated tokens than CoT [c1626].

**Comparison.** All three spend extra computation at inference, but differently: CoT spends it on a single reasoning chain; CoT-SC spends it on multiple independent chains aggregated by vote; ToT spends it on branching, self-evaluated search over intermediate states [c1580][c1576]. The cited ToT experiments are limited to three relatively simple tasks, and the authors note that deliberate search may be unnecessary for many tasks GPT-4 already handles well [c1620]. The library does not directly compare ToT against CoT-SC at matched compute, so claims about which is more efficient per token cannot be drawn from these passages.

sentence_verdicts.text: **Research brief: extra inference-time computation in chain-of-thought (CoT), self-consistency, and Tree of Thoughts (ToT)**
**Chain-of-thought prompting.** CoT elicits intermediate natural-language reasoning steps via few-shot exemplars, which lets a model allocate more computation to harder problems [c1269][c1262].

The authors ablated this: a variant emitting only dots equal to the equation length (variable compute without reasoning) performed about the same as the baseline, suggesting that the benefit comes from expressing intermediate steps in language rather than from extra tokens alone [c1283].
**Self-consistency (CoT-SC).** Rather than greedily decoding one reasoning path, self-consistency samples a diverse set of reasoning paths and takes a majority vote over final answers [c1380][c1386].
The authors report that performance rises with more sampled paths, and that in practice a small number (e.g., 5 or 10) can realize most of the gains while limiting cost [c1421][c1401].
It outperforms beam search under matched numbers of paths, because beam search yields less output diversity [c1408].
Self-consistency also improved GSM8K accuracy over greedy decoding on PaLM-540B, reaching 74.4% [c1432].

**Tree of Thoughts.** ToT treats problem solving as search over a tree whose nodes are partial solutions, with the LM generating candidate next "thoughts," evaluating states, and running search (BFS or DFS) with lookahead and backtracking [c1576][c1582][c1583].
Unlike CoT-SC, which votes over complete chains and has no local exploration within a chain [c1580], ToT explores alternative intermediate steps and can prune or backtrack [c1588].
On Game of 24, ToT achieved a 74% success rate, versus 4% for GPT-4 with CoT [c1573][c1597].

**Cost trade-off.** ToT is substantially more expensive: in Game of 24 it needed about 5.5k completion tokens per problem, close to 100 CoT trials, yet still outperformed the best of 100 independent CoT samples [c1626].
The authors describe cost as highly dependent on prompts and search algorithms, potentially 5–100 times more generated tokens than CoT [c1626].

**Comparison.** All three spend extra computation at inference, but differently: CoT spends it on a single reasoning chain; CoT-SC spends it on multiple independent chains aggregated by vote; ToT spends it on branching, self-evaluated search over intermediate states [c1580][c1576].
The cited ToT experiments are limited to three relatively simple tasks, and the authors note that deliberate search may be unnecessary for many tasks GPT-4 already handles well [c1620].

**Switch Transformer.** The library mentions the Switch Transformer only in passing. The library does not describe how the Switch Transformer routes tokens to experts or how it balances load across them, so those parts of the task cannot be answered from the provided evidence.

**Mixtral.** The library covers Mixtral only as a model evaluated for quantization. [c3869] describes Mixtral as one of the most popular open-source Mixture-of-Experts models, with AWQ achieving superior performance on it. Neither passage describes Mixtral's gating or routing function, the number of experts selected per token, or any load-balancing method. The library does not cover these details.

**Comparison.** Because the library lacks routing and load-balancing descriptions for both models, a direct comparison cannot be made from the evidence. The one shared fact the passages support is that both are sparse Mixture-of-Experts models (Fedus et al., 2021 [c3291][c2988]; Jiang et al., 2024 [c3862][c3869]). Any claims about routing rules, auxiliary balancing losses, or capacity limits would need sources beyond this library.
